items.title: $71,356 and a Lifetime Ban: How George Santos Became Kalshi's Toughest Insider-Trading Case Yet
items.body:
## A Record Penalty for a Familiar Name

Prediction market platform Kalshi has issued its most severe enforcement action to date, permanently banning former U.S. Congressman George Santos from its exchange and ordering him to forfeit more than $71,000 in trading proceeds. According to Kalshi, the action followed an internal investigation into unusual betting activity tied to contracts about Santos's own attendance at a State of the Union address — a case the company describes as the clearest example yet of the kind of insider-style manipulation its compliance team was built to catch.

Santos, who represented New York's 3rd congressional district before being expelled from the House in late 2023, has since become a recurring figure in national headlines over unrelated legal matters. His name resurfacing in connection with a prediction-market enforcement case adds an unusual twist to an already unusual political story — this time centered not on Capitol Hill, but on the fast-growing world of regulated event trading.

## What Kalshi Says Happened

Kalshi operates markets where users can trade contracts tied to the outcome of real-world events, including political occurrences such as whether a specific public figure will attend a scheduled event. Under the platform's rules, individuals with direct, non-public knowledge of their own plans are barred from trading on contracts where that knowledge gives them an unfair edge over the rest of the market — a standard modeled loosely on insider-trading protections in traditional financial markets.

Kalshi says its review found that positions linked to Santos were placed on contracts predicting his own presence at the address, using information about his plans that was not available to other traders at the time. Because the outcome hinged on a decision only Santos himself controlled, the company classified the activity as a clear-cut violation of its market-integrity rules rather than a case of lucky or well-informed speculation.

As a result, Kalshi says it moved to void the profits tied to the trades, impose the $71,356 forfeiture, and bar Santos from ever holding an account on the platform again — a permanent ban that the company says is reserved for its most serious integrity violations.

## Why This Matters for Prediction Markets

Event-contract platforms like Kalshi have expanded rapidly in the United States after receiving regulatory clearance to offer trading on political, economic, and cultural outcomes. That growth has brought closer scrutiny from regulators and the public alike, with critics questioning whether such markets can reliably police conflicts of interest involving the very people whose actions determine an outcome.

Cases like this one are likely to be cited by both supporters and skeptics of prediction markets. Proponents argue that a swift, transparent enforcement response — complete with a public penalty and a permanent ban — shows the self-policing model can work without waiting for a government agency to intervene. Skeptics counter that if a sitting or former public official can attempt to profit from a market tied to their own conduct, it raises broader questions about how well these platforms can prevent insiders from gaming markets tied to their own decisions.

## The Broader Context

Kalshi has positioned itself as a regulated alternative to informal betting markets, operating under oversight from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Company representatives have said in public statements that maintaining trust in market integrity is essential to the platform's long-term legitimacy, particularly as it seeks to expand into more politically sensitive contract categories.

For Santos, the ban adds a new chapter to a public profile already defined by scrutiny over past conduct. Neither Kalshi nor representatives for Santos have detailed further steps, and it remains unclear whether the matter will draw additional regulatory attention beyond the platform's own enforcement action.

As prediction markets continue to attract mainstream attention and investment, cases like this one are expected to shape how platforms write and enforce the rules meant to keep insiders from turning their private knowledge into a market advantage.

items.title: 55.6 and a Four-Year High: Why Factories Are Hiring Again as Tuesday's August PMI Reading Lands
items.body:
## A Surprisingly Strong Month for American Factories

U.S. manufacturers just turned in their best performance in more than four years. The closely watched factory activity index climbed to 55.6 in July, comfortably above the 50-point line that separates expansion from contraction, and marked the strongest reading the sector has produced in over four years. Perhaps more notably, factories added workers to payrolls for the first time in a year and a half — a signal that plant managers see enough demand ahead to justify bringing people back onto the floor rather than just running existing crews harder.

That combination — accelerating output plus renewed hiring — is what has economists and market watchers paying close attention to Tuesday's August reading. A single strong month can be noise. A second one in a row starts to look like a trend.

## Why the Jobs Number Matters More Than the Headline Figure

Manufacturing employment has been sluggish for a while, weighed down by high borrowing costs, cautious capital spending, and inventory drawdowns that let companies meet orders without adding staff. When a purchasing managers' survey shows the employment subcomponent moving back into growth territory, it typically means order books have filled up enough that existing staff and overtime hours are no longer sufficient.

In practical terms, that can show up in a few places worth watching over the coming weeks:

- **Regional Federal Reserve surveys** (Philadelphia, New York, Richmond, Kansas City) often preview or confirm national trends a few weeks before the broader data catches up.
- **Weekly jobless claims**, particularly any softening in claims tied to durable-goods manufacturers.
- **Capital equipment orders**, since factories rarely add headcount unless they're also confident enough to invest in machinery and materials.

## What Could Have Driven the Rebound

A few threads commonly get cited when manufacturing data turns higher after a long soft patch:

1. **Inventory restocking.** After a stretch of destocking, some sectors — autos, electronics components, industrial equipment — may simply need to rebuild inventory levels, which shows up as a temporary but real boost to new orders.
2. **Reshoring and supply-chain adjustments.** Some companies have continued shifting production or sourcing decisions closer to home in response to tariff policy and shipping disruptions of recent years, which can lift domestic order books even if global demand is flat.
3. **Easier financial conditions.** If borrowing costs have eased or are expected to ease, capital-intensive manufacturers tend to green-light projects that were shelved during tighter periods.

None of these are confirmed as *the* explanation — they're simply the usual suspects economists look at first when a factory index jumps.

## The Case for Caution

Not every strong PMI print holds up. A few reasons observers are treating July's number carefully rather than declaring a full recovery:

- **One month is not a trend.** Manufacturing surveys are diffusion indexes based on sentiment among purchasing managers, and they can swing month to month based on a handful of large firms' order timing.
- **New tariffs or input-cost changes** can push prices-paid components higher even when actual output growth is modest, which sometimes flatters the headline number without reflecting broad-based strength.
- **Hiring lags demand by design.** Employers often wait for a few months of confirmed order growth before adding permanent staff, so it's worth watching whether the July hiring uptick was concentrated in temporary workers or overtime versus permanent additions.

## What Tuesday's Report Will Tell Us

The August reading due out Tuesday is effectively a confirmation test. If the index holds near or above the 55 level and the employment component stays positive, it would suggest the July jump wasn't a one-off — supporting the idea that the industrial side of the economy is genuinely turning a corner after a prolonged slowdown. A pullback toward the 50 line, on the other hand, wouldn't necessarily mean the rebound is over, but it would raise the odds that July was driven by temporary restocking rather than a durable pickup in demand.

Either way, the manufacturing sector's health matters well beyond factory floors. It feeds into broader employment reports, regional economies built around industrial hubs, and the outlook that policymakers use when weighing future interest-rate decisions. For now, the data offers a reason for cautious optimism — with Tuesday's number set to show whether that optimism is justified.

*This article is for general informational purposes and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Economic data is subject to revision.*

items.title: More Than 500 Towns Are Blocking AI Data Centers — And Washington Is Worried About Falling Behind China
items.body:
## A Grassroots Revolt Against the AI Boom

Across the United States, a quiet but fast-growing rebellion is taking shape. According to tracking by local-government watchdogs and reported by multiple outlets, more than 500 cities, counties, and townships have moved this year to block, pause, or heavily restrict new artificial intelligence data centers in their communities. That is a striking number for a technology that, just a few years ago, most local officials had never heard of.

The reasons vary from town to town, but a few themes repeat almost everywhere:

- **Electricity costs.** Large AI data centers can consume as much power as a mid-sized city, and residents in several states have reported noticeably higher utility bills after a facility moved in nearby.
- **Grid strain.** Utility operators have warned that clusters of data centers are straining transmission infrastructure that was never designed for this kind of concentrated demand.
- **Water use.** Many facilities rely on water-intensive cooling systems, raising concerns in drought-prone regions.
- **Noise and land use.** Round-the-clock cooling fans and diesel backup generators have drawn complaints in residential and semi-rural areas alike.

For many local officials, the calculus is simple: the jobs and tax revenue a data center brings often don't outweigh the strain it puts on shared infrastructure that everyday residents depend on.

## The White House Pushes Back

The Trump administration has framed the AI buildout very differently — as a matter of national competitiveness. Officials have argued that the United States is locked in a race with China to dominate artificial intelligence infrastructure, and that every blocked project is, in effect, a gift to a strategic rival.

President Trump has been blunt about the stakes, reportedly warning that communities which reject data centers and the power generation needed to run them risk being left "backwards and poor" while other regions — and other countries — capture the economic upside of the AI era. The administration has floated a broader energy and permitting push, sometimes described by supporters under banners like "let data reign," aimed at speeding up approvals for data centers, power plants, and the transmission lines that connect them.

Administration officials argue that AI leadership is inseparable from energy policy: without a rapid buildout of generation capacity — including natural gas, nuclear, and grid upgrades — the U.S. simply cannot host the computing power that next-generation AI models require.

## Local Control vs. National Strategy

The clash highlights a familiar but increasingly consequential tension in American governance: who gets to decide where critical infrastructure goes — the federal government pursuing a national strategic goal, or the local communities that live with the day-to-day consequences?

Supporters of local bans and moratoriums say they are not opposed to AI or economic growth in principle. Many argue they simply want stronger guarantees — on electricity rates, water rights, and long-term environmental impact — before signing off on projects that can operate for decades. Some towns have passed temporary pauses rather than outright bans, giving officials time to study the impact before large projects break ground.

Industry groups and some economists counter that a patchwork of hundreds of local restrictions could slow the U.S. AI buildout at exactly the moment global competition is intensifying, potentially pushing investment toward states — or countries — with fewer regulatory hurdles.

## What Happens Next

Neither side shows signs of backing down. Data center developers continue to court states and counties with tax incentives, while an increasing number of local governments are drafting stricter zoning rules, moratoriums, or ballot measures aimed at slowing new projects until questions about power and water use are resolved.

The outcome of this standoff could shape more than just where the next generation of AI infrastructure gets built. It may also determine how much say ordinary communities retain over projects that promise national economic benefits but often deliver local costs first. As the debate plays out in city council chambers and state legislatures nationwide, it is increasingly being treated as a preview of a much larger question: how the U.S. balances rapid technological ambition with the everyday concerns of the towns being asked to host it.
